texts.preamble: Sreedharan vs George Kutty on 30 June, 2015 Author: K.Ramakrishnan Bench: P.N.Ravindran, K.Ramakrishnan In The High Court Of Kerala At Ernakulam Present: The Honourable Mr.Justice P.N.Ravindran & The Honourable Mr. Justice K.Ramakrishnan Friday, The 6Th Day Of October 2017/14Th Aswina, 1939 RCRev..No. 262 of 2015 () --------------------------
texts.facts: The landlord had in the petition for eviction averred that he had purchased the petition schedule shop room as per Ext.A2 sale deed dated 22.9.2004, that he had thereafter let it out on a monthly rent of Rs.1,000/- to the tenant for the purpose of running a business in vegetables and that the tenant has kept the rent in arrears from September, 2006 onwards. He had also averred that he is working in the Pastry Department of a restaurant in Saudi Arabia and he intends to come back and settle down in his home town by starting a bakery business. He had further averred that he needs the petition schedule shop room to run a bakery, that he has no other suitable building in the locality to run the bakery business, that there are several vacant shop rooms available in Haripad Grama Panchayat for the tenant to shift his business, that the notice issued to the tenant calling upon him to surrender vacant possession of the shop room was returned unserved for the reason that he is working abroad and that he reliably understands that the tenant has sub let the petition schedule shop room to another person without his consent and knowledge. 3. Upon receipt of notice, the tenant filed objections contending inter alia that he has not kept the rent in arrears, that at the time of entrustment in the year 1992 he had paid the sum of Rs.60,000/- as advance to the then owner, that the landlord had not informed him about the fact that he had purchased the building, that there is no rental agreement between him and the landlord, that the petition schedule shop room is not suitable for conducting a bakery business, that on the immediate northern side of the petition schedule shop room another bakery is being run and that the attempt of the landlord is only to evict him from the petition schedule shop room and to let it out to other persons on enhanced rent. He further contended that the landlord has got his own shop rooms at Karthikappally, that he is depending for his livelihood on the income derived from the business carried on in the petition schedule shop room and that no other shop rooms are available in the locality to shift his business. He contended that he has not sub let the petition schedule shop room Sreedharan vs George Kutty on 30 June, 2015 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/140421644/ 2 as alleged by the landlord and that the need put forward is not bonafide. He contended that he is entitled to the protection of the second proviso to section 11(3) of the Act. 4. Initially, the tenant was set ex-parte and an ex-parte order of eviction was passed on 29.9.2007. The tenant thereupon filed I.A.No.553 of 2008 to [LEAKAGE_MASK] the ex-parte order of eviction accompanied by I.A.No.554 of 2008 to condone the delay of 154 days in filing the former application. The Rent Control Court dismissed the said applications by order passed on 31.3.2009. The tenant thereupon filed R.C.A.Nos.20 and 29 of 2009 on the file of the Court of the Rent Control Appellate Authority, Mavelikkara. By judgment delivered on 24.2.2010 the Rent Control Appellate Authority allowed the appeals and [LEAKAGE_MASK] the ex-parte order of eviction subject to payment of Rs.3,000/- as costs. Though the landlord filed R.C.R.Nos.145 and 151 of 2010 in this court, they were dismissed by order passed on 18.8.2010. This court also directed the rent control court to try and dispose of the petition for eviction within four months. 5. Before the Rent Control Court, the brother and power of attorney of the landlord was examined as PW1, two neighbouring shop keepers were examined as Pws.2 and 3, the Tahsildar, Karthikappally who was also the Accommodation Controller was examined as PW4 and the Secretary of the S.N.D.P. Taluk Union, Karkithakappally Taluk was examined as PW5. The landlord also produced and marked Exts.A1 to A11. On application filed by the landlord an Advocate Commissioner was appointed to inspect the petition schedule shop room and also to report about the availability of vacant shop rooms in the locality. The Advocate Commissioner thus appointed was examined as PW6 and the report and mahazar submitted by him were marked as Exts.C1 and C1(a) respectively. On application filed by the landlord, the register maintained by the Accommodation Controller, Karthikappally Taluk was produced by PW4 and marked as Ext.X1. The tenant examined himself as DW1.After considering the rival contentions the rent control court held that the need put forward is bonafide. An order of eviction under section 11(3) of the Act was accordingly passed on 29.2.2012 directing the tenant to surrender vacant possession of the petition schedule shop room within three months from the date of the order. Challenging that order, the tenant filed R.C.A.No.3 of 2012 on the file of the Rent Control Appellate Authority, Mavelikkara. By judgment delivered on 30.6.2015 the Rent Control Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal. The tenant has aggrieved thereby, filed this revision petition under section 20 of the Act.
texts.arguments: 6. The main ground raised in the instant revision petition is that the Rent Control Court and the Appellate Authority erred in passing an order of eviction under section 11(3) of the Act, relying on the testimony tendered by the power of attorney holder of the landlord examined as PW1. It is contended that as the landlord has not entered the box and has not spoken to the need set out by him, an order of eviction under section 11(3) of the Act could not have been passed. The tenant also contends that the need put forward is not bonafide, that the landlord has failed to establish his intention to come back and settle in India and that he is entitled to the protection of the second proviso to section 11(3) of the Act. Sreedharan vs George Kutty on 30 June, 2015 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/140421644/ 3 7. After the revision petition was admitted and the respondent landlord entered appearance, he filed I.A.No.2995 of 2015 to reopen the evidence in O.P.(R.C.)No.2 of 2007 and to permit him to examine himself as PW7 and to produce additional evidence. He had in the affidavit filed in support of the said application averred that as he was employed abroad his brother and power of attorney was prosecuting the case on his behalf on the strength of Ext.A1 power of attorney executed by him on 23.9.2004, that Pws.1 to 6 were examined before he came back to India on 2.2.2012 after resigning his employment abroad, that thereafter his passport was produced and marked as Ext.A11 by consent and that it was on account of the fact that he was employed abroad and came back to India only on 2.2.2012, that he could not enter the box and tender evidence. He had also averred that arguments in the case were heard by the Rent Control Court on 16.2.2012 and that after arriving in India he has taken a room on rent and is running a bakery therein under the name and style 'A-One Bakery'. He had along with I.A.No.2995 of 2015 filed an affidavit in lieu of chief examination and produced along with it documents to prove the averments in the said affidavit. 8. The tenant opposed the said application by filing written objections. He contended that no exceptional circumstances exist so as to warrant reopening of the evidence for the purpose of examining the landlord as PW7. He contended that from the very fact that Ext.A11 was produced and marked before the Rent Control Court, it is evident that the landlord could have, if he was desirous of doing so, entered the box and testified. He contended that as the landlord was not denied an opportunity to testify, there is no reason to reopen the evidence. Relying on Rule 16 of Order XVIII of the Code of Civil Procedure, the tenant contended that the landlord could have requested the Rent Control Court to record his evidence before leaving for his place of employment abroad and therefore for that reason also, the relief prayed for in the application cannot be granted. Learned counsel for the revision petitioner contended that even going by the evidence tendered by the landlord examined as PW7, the case put forward by him in the petition for eviction has not been established. Learned counsel contended that the landlord has not proved that he is actually running a bakery business, that the evidence adduced by the landlord will prove that he is running only a catering business and therefore, no reliance can be placed on the testimony tendered by the landlord examined as PW7 or the documents produced and marked as Exts.A12 to A16 to sustain the order of eviction. Learned counsel contended that even the additional evidence adduced in this court would not justify an order of eviction. 11. Per contra, learned counsel for the respondent submitted that the main ground put forward in the revision petition is that the rent control court could not have passed an order of eviction as the landlord has not entered the box and testified. Learned counsel contended that the main case set out Sreedharan vs George Kutty on 30 June, 2015 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/140421644/ 5 in the revision petition is that as the landlord has failed to establish his intention to come back to India and to start a bakery business, an order of eviction could not have been passed. Learned counsel for the landlord submitted that the evidence now adduced before this court would show that after the landlord came back to India on 2.2.2012, he had taken a room on rent and is running a bakery therein. Learned counsel contended that in such circumstances, no interference is called for with the order of eviction passed by the Rent Control Court and the judgment delivered by the Rent Control Appellate Authority upholding the order of eviction.
